request.lesson: Python's $ matches before a trailing newline and \d accepts Unicode decimal digits, so an identifier regex anchored with ^...$ fails open. When the validated string is later compared by exact equality against persisted state, x:1, x:1 with a trailing newline, and x:01 are three spellings of one identity that all pass and compare unequal, defeating an idempotency guard. Use \A and \Z, an explicit 0-9 class, a length cap, and a canonical-form check whenever the validated value is compared as a string.

The shipped acceptance-criteria guidance now enforces this lesson directly. The spec template requires that every numeric limit record the input that makes it fire first and the enforcement mechanism that makes that ordering true, that two limits on one quantity are either ordered so each is reachable or one is declared non-binding, that a limit names the reference point it is measured from and chooses an origin giving the same input the same measurement however the subject is organised, and that a criterion requiring a limit states its value rather than asking an implementer to supply one. The rule is in the artifact an author reads while writing, so the topic is no longer the place the lesson lives.

A document-wide href scan over an emitted Starlight page cannot prove a link exists in a particular section, because Starlight renders the full guide sidebar on every page. A case asserting that the relocated catalogue-extension section still linked to its four guides passed under a mutation that deleted one of those step links, because the sidebar carried the same href. It only failed once scoped to the section's own nodes. Two mechanics make the scoping work: heading ids resolve through a wrapper, since Starlight emits <div class="sl-heading-wrapper level-hN"> around each heading and section content are siblings of that WRAPPER, not of the heading -- walking the heading's own siblings yields only the anchor icon and an empty section. And Starlight's slug is not the obvious one: '### P2 · Shape what to build — ~3 hours' emits id="p2--shape-what-to-build--3-hours", because github-slugger drops the punctuation and keeps the spaces that surrounded it, so a slugifier collapsing whitespace runs to one hyphen derives a different anchor than the site serves.

tools/build-site.py rewrites an unresolvable in-tree Markdown link into an external GitHub blob locator, which moves it out of tools/check-rendered-site-links.py's scope because that audit checks internal links only. A mistyped in-repo link therefore ships as an external 404 while the gate stays green. Measured on 2026-09-09: guides/desk-research/ carried six unresolvable relative .md links -- README.md naming how-to/desk-research-pipelines.md and explanation/desk-research-methodology.md when the files are research-pipelines.md and research-methodology.md, and your-first-research-project.md naming research-first-session.md when the file is desk-research-first-session.md -- while make site-link-check reported 73,075 links across 288 pages clean. The emitted page carried an external blob locator pointing back at the non-existent guides/ path. Detect this class from both sides: walk authored guides/ links against the filesystem, and assert no emitted page carries an external blob locator pointing back under guides/. A clean site-link-check is not evidence that in-tree guide links resolve.

A SAST gate that turns the scanner's own diagnostics into a failure signal reds on files the diff never touched when the host is contended. Semgrep run with --strict exits non-zero on a per-file time-budget breach, not only on a finding, so several tools gating at once on one machine fail the build on unrelated code. The discriminator is that the timed-out file set reshuffles between runs: a real defect names the same file every time, a budget breach names different files and a count that tracks load rather than the diff. Observed across four runs of one unchanged tree: 3 timeouts on one file, then 14 across six files, then 3 again, then 0 and a clean exit, at load 95 to 226 on 10 cores. Diagnose it by checking load, confirming the named file is absent from the diff, and running the exact failing invocation against that file alone -- it exits 0. The repair is to re-run when the machine is quiet, or to pin or vendor the unpinned registry rulesets whose rules are the ones timing out. Do not widen the scanner's exclude list: that trades a transient failure for a permanent blind spot, and it needs a stated residual and a retirement trigger. Do not report the gate green on the strength of a single passing re-run either -- report the count, the load and the varying file set.

When a spec or plan clause has produced a sustained review finding twice, delete it rather than reword it a third time. Two clauses each generated a finding under two successive wordings: a boundary scope gloss that first forbade the surfaces the durable-output table assigns and then, reworded, made that table a write allowlist and forbade every working surface the tasks construct; and a durable-output row whose partial task list was wrong under every subset because every task produced the evidence. Deletion cost nothing because another surface already owned the fact. The wider pattern: after the first review round, most sustained findings were introduced by earlier repairs, so after changing a rule check the surface you did not touch, not the one you did. The three that recurred were a criterion whose selector moved while a task still selected by the old predicate, a task whose approach changed without its tests, and an accounting row that had to list a newly added producer.

Plan a corpus change against the projected tree, not the authored one. Two owner-authorized amendments in one delivery came from the same blind spot: the anchor-test sweep checked digests and counts over authored sources, while two separate shipped guards scan the compiled projection. One requires a doctrine group's provenance block to appear in the compiled body, so the first task adding such a group cannot pass without a recompile; the other forbids delivery-mechanic literals anywhere in the projected tree, so a criterion requiring one was unsatisfiable and only failed after the recompile made it visible. A third consequence follows from the first: because the compiled source digest binds recorded evaluation runs, the recompile and the re-measurement must travel inside the task that makes the last authored edit, since a separate later task can never share its wave and gates run at wave boundaries.

A prose-containment assertion over a governed document is discharged by any second copy of the same sentence in that document. Three separate controls in one delivery could not fail for this reason: a verification-date check satisfied by the block's own source retrieval dates, then by a source's exposed last-updated date after the first repair, and a placement check satisfied by the provenance block that restates every clause verbatim. The shape is always the same — the assertion reads the whole artifact while the property is about one region of it. Scope the read to the region the property is about, and prove the repair by measuring the old and new predicates on the same mutated state rather than by asserting the fix. When a document deliberately restates its claims for provenance, treat the restatement as a second surface, not as redundant text.

A review round's finding set measures where its brief pointed, not what is wrong with the artifact. Round 8 of one spec sustained a stale cross-reference that had been present and reachable for at least two earlier rounds; it surfaced only because that round's brief named reference-walking as its first attack. Two consequences. A declining per-round finding count partly measures brief narrowing rather than rising artifact quality, so it is not on its own evidence of convergence. And a round that says nothing about an area is not evidence that area is clean. Keep this separate from the illegitimate case: a reviewer reopening a decision the brief records as settled is not a late finding, and is refused rather than repaired.

A helper that takes a directory and shells out to git must be asserted against a real repository subdirectory, not only a temporary fixture. Git resolves a pathspec relative to the current directory rather than the repository root, so listing a tree with a root-relative pathspec while the working directory is inside that same directory searches for it nested under itself, matches nothing, and exits zero. There is no error to catch, and a best-effort wrapper reads the empty result as 'nothing on the remote'. Run the call from the repository root and keep the pathspec root-relative, or ask the lister for the full tree. The defect survived review and a green suite because the fixture built its records at the repository root, where the relative path is empty and the pathspec degrades to the current directory, which is the one shape where the two coincide and no real caller is shaped that way. A fixture whose directory layout differs from production is exercising a different function; one assertion against the real tree is cheaper than the suite that missed it.
